segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I appreciate you coming. As we begin, first I am going to tell you the reason that we are doing this. You do know that they are learning, I guess you could say adults and little ones. One of these days, they are going to start listening to Cherokee. I don't know if they will make it that far, but I believe they want to advance that far. They are going to listen to it someday, and another reason is that if you have grandkids, or if you have kids, one day we are all going to pass on. They may one day want to hear you talking and they will allow them to listen. As we begin, first tell me your full English name?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Kenneth Littledeer.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Norma Littledeer.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What is your name in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I really don't know. Mom used to tell me a lot. ᎢᏌᎦ ᎨᏁ what is it she used to say? I forget. Mom used to say she really didn't know, but she used to tell me a lot.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I forget, too.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: ᎪᏴᏂ.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: ᎪᏴᏂ.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Who are your parents?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Roy and Inole Grimmett.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, is that right?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Roy came, and he said he didn't even want to leave here. “I feel good,” he said. I said, “Dad, you went in there a long time. You went in there for an hour. He said, “Some go in and come right back out.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was enjoying it.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, he said he was enjoying it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That's good.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: He don't hardly have anyone to talk to since Mom passed away. He just keeps to himself a little bit.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Does he still go to church at Sequoyah?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: From time to time. It's his eye.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: He just has one eye now. He lost one.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Ohhh.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: He's blind in one eye.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many were in your family, you?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Me and Norma.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I think in your family...your mom...

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Me, my mom, and my sister.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Four of you? Oh, just three.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you all speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: No, no, my one sister, she didn't want to. She didn't listen to Mom talking Cherokee to her.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was that the last born?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah. It's changed really quick, ain't it? From watching TV. Linda was my mom, Linda Littledeer.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Linda... Oh Linda Littledeer. I know her, but I've known Roy a long time.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: ᎦᏖ was her name.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How about you? How many were in your family?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Aye, at least 10.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: There were 10 of you?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: 11? Let me see. Seven girls and three boys.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: One of the boys is named Roy, too, ain't it?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, Roy, Marco, and then Frank; he passed away.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That little boy, I don't think they're gonna have that team this year that they had. Roy and his son, Winterhawk. They said they're not gonna coach a team. He was funny that boy named Winterhawk. He was calling him, and one day I listened good, he was calling him Winterhog.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Winterhog.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: He's a real friendly boy.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, he's a friendly boy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, he's good.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: He tries everything Cherokees do.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: At the house.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I don't even know if he speaks Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No, sometimes, but he don't speak as much as we do. He'll say one or two words.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: That's what I was thinking on our way up here. Nobody taught us Cherokee, we just heard it. Every day, that's all they talked.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Just from speaking.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: That's all they spoke at the house.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: When we started school, English was hard. Those English things.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: If they learn it like that, they can speak like we do.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: To listen good. Didn't your dad...

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I didn't know my dad.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about your mom, what did she do to provide for you all?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: She didn't have to worry. She was handicapped.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Ohh.
Seizures.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: She had seizures all the time. She went through it bad but she depended on God all the time.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: She said she depended on him.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: She was pretty old when she broke her hip. We thought she was gonna see bad times, but in just a little while she was walking around.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I really am glad God had compassion for her. She could walk again. She was living alone. My sister was staying there, and she urged her to move because she said she wasn’t able to take care of herself. When she stayed there, she said, “I can't do anything. She is always standing there, ‘Don't, Granny. Here, Granny.’”

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Don't be eating this, Granny.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: She was told not to eat certain foods; she was eating too many snacks. She was wanting sour… uh… sweets. I'm trying to say sweets. She wanted something sweet all the time. They were telling her not to and she was getting mad.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Ah mom.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: She didn't like it a little bit, them telling her what to do.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you go to school?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: At Dahlonegah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you finish there?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Then I started at Stilwell High School. I finished there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you started at Dahlonegah, did you already speak good English?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You didn't have a hard time.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, it was really hard, I had a hard time reading things. It was hard for me to read and learn anything. I learned numbers, but to read, I couldn't do it. And that spelling, I couldn't do it. I really barely finished high school. And it was only because Mom pleaded with me.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: When the bus was coming near, she would say, “Get up! The bus is coming right there,” she would say. She hit him with her fist, he said.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about that - what would you call it? spelling?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I don't know, I guess just write, is all I would say.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I would say just learning to write.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: As for me, ᏓᏂ-spelling-ᏲᏍᏗᎲ.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: ᏓᏂ-spelling-ᏲᏍᏗᎲ haw.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I've never heard that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That's what I've heard. ᏓᏂ-spelling-ᏲᏍᏗᎲ.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Mom knew all the months. Every month she would tell me what month it is.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: In Cherokee?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, in Cherokee. Boy, I feel bad because I can't remember those. I can forget things pretty quick. Even if someone tells me their name, I will forget.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I'll tell y'all the truth, when I walk out of here later and my wife says, “Who did you talk to?” I will have already forgotten.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Already, yeah, yeah. I'm the same way.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I tried to remember, and at first, I remembered what Mom used to tell me. She would say, “It is this [gestures] month.” I didn't even know she could read Cherokee. One time, she gave me money for a school trip. We were in eighth grade, we went to Sequoyah’s home. And the money that she gave me, I bought her a Cherokee Bible, I think it was written in Cherokee. And I gave it to her and she said, “Oo wee, I don't know how to read this.” I also bought another one that had the syllabary in it. She started herself, and before long she started reading Cherokee - that Cherokee Bible. She sounded pretty reading it.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah Mom, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You never learned?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I never learned to read but I would want to. I was telling my wife I have to be brave and do that. Because I really want to learn how to read.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That's another reason why I think - I don't know if it's right, this school here. When they start to read and learn, I believe they could eventually speak the way we do.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah. It's cute when they talk.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you, where did you go to school?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I started at Maryetta. Well, Bell, then Maryetta. Then I started at Dahlonegah in the sixth grade. I finished there, then Stilwell.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was the reason you started at Bell?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: My aunt, ᏥᏂᏏ, she raised us, that one.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: For 10 years. We were seven to 12 years old, and Mom got us back, and we went to Dahlonegah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh. Who was born first, you or Roy?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I don't think he can talk Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I haven't heard him when he was around.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: They try. They can understand, you know. They know, but they can't speak it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: See, I didn't know Roy was Winterhawk’s dad.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Oh, you didn't.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Then one day he called him Dad. Then I thought that. He’s a little bit like my sons, Winterhawk.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Oh, is that right? That's good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When he borrows something, he won't bring it back.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: That's the way they are.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He borrowed a trailer about two weeks ago, and he still has it.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: What about you, what's your name?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Charlie Shell.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Charlie Shell.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I thought you knew.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I didn't recognize you.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I pastor at ᏧᏲᎱᏒ. You know where ᏧᏲᎱᏒ is, right?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Belfonte.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Oh, is that right? Oh, it’s there? It's been a long time since I've been that way.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Like I was saying earlier, we had a wild onion dinner on Sunday.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Gah-lee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We had lots of wild onion piled up.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Oh, that's delicious. She was telling me we just need to buy some.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: My wife still has half a bag to fix. She preserves it.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Your wife, did she used to sell Avon?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: She didn't, it must be a different one.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Mom got sick on me last year.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: July 23rd.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: But she started getting sick in June.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, June.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: She had surgery three times. She has that thing on, right now.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: That bag.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: That's what she's waiting for.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: April 4th they're gonna fix it.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: They said it would be just six weeks. Something went wrong and she got worse, but we prayed and we were asking for prayers.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, prayers are strong. Did you have cancer?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You didn't?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: It was the intestines.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, they got a lot off.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: My wife had something like that. She had cancer, but they took it off.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah, I'm in a hurry for that.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, we were hunting onions all the time, and we liked going fishing. It's been about a year since we’ve done anything, ain't it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When I said my wife had cancer, she was in Ft Smith for about a year, if you counted all of it. We lived there at the doctor.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: It's bad to live there, ain't it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: “Mrs Shell, we're just about gonna kill you before we make you better.” So, she got really sick.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I think I know you.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Diane.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Marie.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Diane. Marie is the baby.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, is that you? Oh my gosh. I thought I knew her when I looked at her. We played, ain't it, we played ball, ain't it? Norm, yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It's been a long time.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You're old, ain't it?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: We used to really like to play ball.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: With Senora Gonzalas and Dave Killer.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was our coach.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, and Charlie. Yeah, I remember that. 12 years old, when I was playing, yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And you, about how old were you?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: About how old were we?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: We were pretty young, ain't it?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We’re still young.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah really, we’re young.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Senora was getting mad at us when we started beating them.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: They got their feelings hurt.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: At first they used to beat us all the time.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, all the time.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: [unintelligible]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Her uncle is Senora.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Oh, OK, and “Too late Vann.”

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: There was a lot.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I had fun a long time ago.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, really, it was fun.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: We went there real slow towards Greasy, there would be a lot of people.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Greasy ballpark.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Some would stay all night, the ones that lived close by. There would be a lot of people all weekend.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, when I think about that, it makes me happy, them days. Makes me happy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Let's back up for a minute. Where did you grow up? Just there in Dahlonegah?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Cherry Tree.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Cherry Tree. What was it like there when you were a child?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: When I was a child, nobody hardly worked, there was nothing to do in Stilwell. We just picked apples and strawberries; it was just, you know, seasonal work.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And beans.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah everything, that was all we knew. You know my family.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Family.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Really, when I was growing up, really, all of my friends, we didn't have dads.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, y'all didn't have dads.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: No, we didn't have dads. That generation, there was a lot, it seemed us friends were. Yeah, us boys couldn't find anything to do. They opened up that Bell boxing, and that Thomas Muskrat helped us a lot.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y'all box?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, we went everywhere, boxing. That's what really helped me, pointed me, and showed me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you learned.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: And Jimmy Hawkins.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, and ball. That was Jim Hawkins. He used to be a cop a long time ago.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: …he took us…

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Baseball?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, baseball.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Me too. I lead an 18-year-old boys' team in Stilwell.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Boy, that’ll take work, ain't it, watching those kids?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Boy, it was funny, we were at Muldrow. Muldrow really liked to cheat. They would cheat you.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: If you let them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I took them there one time, and those women found out because the parents used to go with us all the time. And so, I told them we were going to have to go to Muldrow on Friday. Do you two know Tony Mayness, his son? His son, Chooge.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, Chooge.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He was playing. He started shouting and talking to everybody. “Make sure you all are here and ready to go and tell others about it, we’re going to go to Muldrow.” There were many that went there, but it didn't stop anything, they still cheated us.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Gah-lee, they weren't scared.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I told him I'm gonna protest. “You're going to have to go to that concession and tell them,” he told me. I knew you had to put some money down.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: You had to put it down.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I didn't know how much it was. I went there and when I got there that man was in there and I told him, “I'm going to protest this game.” Maybe he thought, “This guy don't have it.” Maybe he thought I didn't have it. He said, “It's gonna cost you $100 to protest.” The counter went like this [slap]; it made a sound. It was Colbert Starr who laid his checkbook down and said to him, “How much do you need?”

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: “Here you go.”

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Colbert and I were friends back then.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That was his son that was playing ball, James.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, we went to school together.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, I knew James.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, it made that sound [slap] and he wrote him a check pretty quickly. What about you, the same? Did you grow up in Cherry Tree?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, well, and Bell.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Bell?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, but I don't - you know - remember. I don't remember good. I don't know, growing up, what happened. There were 14 of us living in that house.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it a small house back then?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did it have electricity?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, but we didn't have an inside bathroom.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We didn't have water back then. What about you?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I think it was bad.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: And when we washed, we’d wash in the creek water.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Y'all washed at the creek?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Uh-huh, yeah. It was hard, but I don't think about it, I just think it was good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You didn't know you had it hard.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It was the same with me.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, it was good. Happier, I guess.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: If a white person looked at us, they thought we were poor, but we didn't think we were.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: No, it wasn't. I say that all the time, you know.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Nowadays, they wouldn't believe it. Gravy, beans, and bread is all we ate growing up. Sometimes meat, but you know, it was mostly gravy and beans.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: But also, if they could go back, it would be hard for them.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, if they tried to go back and live like we lived..

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It would be hard.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: It would be hard.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was she able to plant a garden?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: She never did. My grandpa used to have a garden.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, he had a garden.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Who was your grandpa?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: ᏫᎵ ᏥᎵ.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, is that right!

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: ᏫᎵ ᎠᏥᎵ.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Boy, that old man, he was crazy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I wasn’t going to say it, but I was thinking it.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: He was funny when he got done griping around.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s how they called him, too, ain’t it, ᏫᎵ ᎠᏥᎵ.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, ᏫᎵ ᎠᏥᎵ.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what I remember. And you, did Roy plant a garden?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Oooh, no!

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He was too lazy!

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Mama did, though.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She had a garden.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: She fixed it. Mama could do everything back then, upholstery, chicken houses, anything.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: She was a builder.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Huh!

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah! You asked her, “Am I going to help you?” “No you’re not going to help me.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Roberta was your aunt, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, Roberta, no, well, Roy is my stepdad.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, Roy’s your stepdad?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, Tommy Sanders is my dad. Yeah, Lyons Switch Donnie, Uncle Donnie.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I thought Roy was your real dad.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: No Tommy Sanders, I think! You know him?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I know him, I’m trying to think of the names of his sons.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Tommy, Shawn… What’s that other one’s name? I forgot what their names are, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Isn’t one's name Tommy, too?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s what I thought. I worked with one of them, Paul Holloway was our boss. But I forgot what his name is.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Tony?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Not Tony? Tony, Tommy, Shawn…

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Tony wouldn’t have been working anywhere…

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: No, he wouldn’t.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: If I remember it, I will tell you.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: What I was talking about, it was hard to find a job in Stilwell. Just at Stilwell Foods.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, that was the only place they had that you could work. And another one was Greenleaf, but we didn’t have cars to go there.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: When I worked there for a little while, I used to ride in the back of the pickup. I rode back there, but I used to pay. Somebody would say, “I’ll give you a ride, but you’re going to have to get in the back.” I said, “That’s good.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I remember I wasn’t working then, but I do remember a little bus that was driving around.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Is that right?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Workers would ride in there.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I do know where they fix chicken, they had some buses, Decatur.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Bentonville.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, one was going that way.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That bus that was going by, I said. There was a guy that lived at Greasy, his name was Charlie Canoe. He worked at Greenleaf, and he said he was really getting tired of always getting a pokesalad sandwich. He said he thought, “When it gets lunchtime, I’m going to hurry up and get there first and trade with somebody else.” So when it made a sound, I went first, and I went like this [gestures], and I was going to choose the heaviest one. And so, I found the heaviest one, and I put my sack up there. I took it, and then the others came. I was watching him, and he was really eating that pokesalad sandwich. I thought it was pretty good that I stole one, now I’m going to eat. When I opened it up, there was a hammer and five hickory nuts!

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Just like ᏍᎦᏰᏥ.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, just like that, huh…

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: That Sassler.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, I know him.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: But he could tell them, too. He told one, one time at school. He said he was going to school, and his mom made him a fried potato and bread sandwich.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Same thing, ain't it, he said.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: He said he just put it in a sack, our lunch sacks. It was almost time to eat. “I'm gonna steal somebody’s lunch, I want something else,” he thought. “I was looking for a fancy lunch box and I grabbed it and took off, and thought, “I'm going to eat good,” he was thinking. He said, “I went and sat under a tree and when I opened it there was a hammer and some hickory nuts.”

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: He told another: one time, there used to be hobos going around.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, they used to walk around on the road.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: He said, “I asked them where they were going and they said, ‘We are going to Kansas and you should go with us.’ I told them, ‘I'll be back.’ I went and got some things, and I put on what they had on, and when I got back, the train was just leaving and I threw my stuff on there and I was running beside it.” He jumped, but his buckle got caught. He ran on the side of that boxcar all the way to Kansas.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He can't not lie, ain't it?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: He said, “One time, I came out of Odies, and there were two men sitting there. They said, ‘Sassler, tell us a good one.’ I said, ‘I ain't got time. My wife is having a baby.’ So the next day, when I got there, they said, ‘Sassler, we didn't know you had a wife.’ I said, ‘Well, you told me to tell you a good one.’”

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Gaw, that was a good one.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: He was a crazy old man.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Roy is the same way, Roy Grimmett. He told about 10 jokes that Sassler told.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Sassler told this, too, he said, “They were playing ball. I was there and they couldn't find a pitcher. I told them I would pitch and they said alright go warm up. I went and put my jacket on and got in the truck and turned on the heater. I was sitting in there, sweating, getting warm.”

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: He was a funny old man.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you learn how to cook? Does she know how?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, I know how. I think my sister Patsy, the oldest one, when she was nine years old, she watched all of us, and cooked. Mama would cook bread and potatoes. Then she would go [gesture], you know. And then there would be, Patsy said, there would be food. About two or three days, there would be quite a bit.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That Patsy, did you learn from watching her?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah, when we got back to Mom’s and then I watched her. It was little bit different. I learned that, too. I was eight, I was able to make biscuits.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, eight years old.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: She's baked a lot of bread.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You also know how to make fried bread?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Oooooh, yeah.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Boy, and I started getting fat, that's what happened to me. And the doctor said, “You're really borderline diabetic now,” he told me. Gaw… she quit frying bread.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: And now, probably once a week.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Every now and then she gives it to me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Man, I couldn't eat without using bread.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: That's what happens to me, too.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Even for me, I really came through a rough time. It's been almost a year. Cause I can't eat bread now. Everything.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I'm a diabetic.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I'm not.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: You’ve lost about 100, huh?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Gaw.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You've lost that much?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, she really got sick. She still has to have surgery. We’re just waiting for her to get better. There's a lot of things she can't do.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What happened to my wife, she was told, “You might have to have that the rest of your life.” Another one said that. But then we talked to the surgeon. She told him what the doctor said to her, and he said, “No, that's not it,” he said. He said to her, “If there is a small chance I can do something, you're not going to do that.” And so, he did surgery. She just had to wear it six weeks, and she had to go back in. And they fixed it.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: For me, it was six weeks also. But it's been eight months now.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: She's still having difficulties. They still have to fix it, they said. They really have to lower it, but it wasn't enough. It has to be here [gestures], and it is hard for her. And also, our boy, the same thing happened to him. He's already had his fixed. How long has he been wearing that?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Seven months.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: He’s worn it for seven months.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: It's that diverticulitis they call it. That's it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's happened to me.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Boy, it's bad.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Boy, I waited too long before I went.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: That boy…

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: …it's painful…

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: …yeah, it's painful…

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: …his exploded. He really almost passed away. We were telling him to go to the doctor and he said it’ll pass. We were pleading with him to go to the doctor. Man, he almost died. That doctor said he got them all out when I took him back. I was talking to that doctor, and he said, “God is good,” he told my boy. “We had you all on the table and cleaned everything inside you.” It blew up, that acid stuff. You would be amazed how God let him do that. Yeah, I mean…

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: …he was standing near, ain't it…

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: … and there was two surgeons…

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: …all the time…

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: …all the time, ain't…

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: …maybe it took about 7 hrs. That's a long time.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Mine was what? Six?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Six. Six and a half that was.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: They were in there a long time.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That's strange. In the past, if you had surgery, you would be in there for about a week, huh?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When I had surgery, I had prostate cancer. They had six incisions this [gestures] long. The next day I was told I could go home.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, that's what they do. That's what they did when I had surgery on my head. I went home the next day.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Why? Did they think you was tough?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s right.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Boy, I thought, I'm gonna be laying here getting fed. You’ll be going home in the morning, they told me.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Not really.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: “Let me stay in a little while.”

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: You could've said “I'm on vacation.”

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Mom also had surgery on her head one time. Boy, she fell down and she wasn't waking up. And the doctor was telling me, over there in Tulsa, “She's not going to wake up if I don't do surgery. Blood will bleed in her head,” he said. I quickly remember what that doctor said, “God is something, God made this our head, here's a bone. That is just like, we could do like he made it, you can take that round bone out. God made it like that, he told me.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: It’s like a puzzle.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: “We can take it out and there will be a hole there, we can get in there,” he told me. But that was the first thing he said, “God is awesome.”

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: He is.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: We are able to do that because the head is a hard thing. But that little spot he made. Where someone could get through…

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: …get through.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The one that did my wife’s surgery, when we first got in there, that’s what we were telling him, the Lord’s going to take care of it. He wouldn't say anything like that, so I thought he didn't believe anything like that. Now, towards the last, she had already had surgery, we were talking and that’s what he said. “The Lord took care of it,” he said.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: That’s true.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Gaw, that's true.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He said that himself. We knew he was going to, my wife said. He took care of it, he said.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah. Mom really did get sick, the doctors were afraid, I could really tell it was scaring them. Some were saying, “Let's pray,” and they were asking us if we wanted to pray. She went through really good, the doctors were really watching her.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: We were always singing and praying. The nurses came in and said “Boy I feel something in here.” It was God.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It's a joyful feeling that it's like that. It's really good.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Boy, you can feel it, they said.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you were growing up, when you all would get sick, did you go to a doctor, or did your grandma or your mom know a little something?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, I went to those that know things all the time. The healers.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The healers. You don't remember a little about what they used?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: That's what I was thinking about. I never paid attention, but I do remember, my grandma, when they got a cold, they would have on top of...

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: On top of the stove.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, I do remember that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: A heat stove.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: It would get warm when you drank.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it bark from a wood, was it like that?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, it was like that. But I don't know what they call it in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Mama would fix it for kidneys, she had it all the time for us girls to drink. I think it was wild cherries?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it the bark?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Have you heard that, something like that for kidney medicine?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Me? No.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: That's what we’ve been asking everybody, if they know anything. We know that long time ago they made it, but...

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: But you two don't remember.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: It was wild cherry, I think. Yeah, Mom was making medicine and things all the time. We didn't hardly go to the doctor.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, you didn't. Do you also not remember anything? That's why we’re losing it, ain't it?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: ..that’s why...

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: ..a lot of Vicks is all I know. A lot of Vicks. And Menthaledom.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Dad was like that.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: She would put some on her finger and put it in my mouth.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You all ate it. Me too. I like eating Vicks.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Even if you're laying there about to die, they would put Vicks in your mouth.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, that's the best kind, they say, Vicks.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I'm the same way, I'll put Vicks everywhere.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Boy, I don't like Vicks.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I do, it makes me feel good.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Her feet.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I put it on my feet, my knees,

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: She’ll go to sleep real quick.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: My arms.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: If you're coughing, there ain't nothing better than Vicks.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: That's true.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: If the kids are coughing all the time.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: And they say coffee and black pepper.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Put in pepper.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Pepper.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: If you're coughing.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, if you lay down and cover up.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That black pepper.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, coffee and black pepper, lay down and put covers on.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's what would make me cough.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: That littlest boy of ours really had a fever, and we didn't know what to do.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: ᏍᎦᏰᏥ told us. ᏳᏫᏍᏗ.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: ᏍᎦᏰᏥ told ᏳᏫᏍᏗ my aunt, and that..

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: His dad.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Back then..

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That's also Sassler, ain't it?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: They had brown paper sacks.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: That's all it was a long time ago.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Mustard.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: He told me to make it this long [gesture], like a strip.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Just fold it and put a lot of mustard in there. If you fold it up and make it like a headband, he told that boy, it would dry it up real quickly, he told him.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: That mustard dried up, and his fever went away.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: It got better right quick.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: That mustard pulled that heat out of his head.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I was amazed.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: He felt good.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: He felt better quickly.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I remember ᏆᎵᏳᎩ, do you remember them? The oldest boy, his tooth was hurting, he had a tooth ache. Well, I told him, let's take him. Boy, that boy got up, ᏆᎵᏳᎩ took a drink of water. He said, “Haw, Mom.” “Haw, babe, what is it?” “You always make me nasty stuff.”

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: When they spit on you.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, when they spit on you.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: “You make me do nasty stuff, Mama.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He was healing him.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Mom knew that, too, when you had fever, she would blow water on you. I don't know what she said, though.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She said something, though, right?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, she was saying something.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: As for me, I don't know if you know Lizzy Proctor, is her name, she helped me with my head.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Oh she's good, she's a good one.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I couldn't go to sleep and I couldn't lay down. And she took me over there, but I don't know if you know Viola Glass, Viola Fourkiller, she took me over there. She told me to sit on this side, so I sit like I'm sitting now. She went and got some water. She was doing that nasty stuff, she was blowing on me, then she said, “When we’re finished, go lay down right there.” And so, that is all I remember is laying down. I woke up four or five hours later, and she told me we were finished. I have never been in pain with my head hurting.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: What about that Terry Mayes, do you know him, he also asked Lizzy, what was it he said?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: It was the same, it was his head.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: He went by there, he said. She made him good, he said. Terry Mayes. He said someone told him to go over there. So he said, “I went there.” She made him good, he said.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He was a really good Cherokee speaker, that Terry.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Oh really, he’s still trying.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He still is.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: That's where we still go to church, Church on the Rock.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, so you go there.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yep, that's where we go to church.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, he was really good speaker.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did he forget?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: He forgot a little bit.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: That's right, he forgot.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He could speak just like a Cherokee back then.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: So, when we first started there, they did not sing Amazing Grace in Cherokee. Then we said we should sing Amazing Grace in English and in Cherokee, so we do that now. And they have all learned it. Becky Scott teaches them,

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: She's really smart, that one.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: As you hear it. “Write down what I'm saying,” she said. Just by hearing it, it will be good.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Write it like you hear, she said. “Write it yourself” and I gave her the pencil, and as she heard it, she wrote it. And then Silent Night.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Silent Night.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Silent Night in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: We sang that, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And in Cherokee, too.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: They can sing it in Cherokee. It's beautiful that Silent Night.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Sing it.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: We don't have a book.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I try, but if I read it, I can remember again pretty quickly, you know, if I read it a little bit.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: It beautiful.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: It sounds beautiful, ain't it?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I was amazed with Becky, with how many people were learning.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When we used to have a family group of singers, I don't know if you remember the Shell family.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, I do.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The Shell family singers. Do you remember that white person, that white woman who used to play music for us? She was just a girl when she started.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Just a little bit, what was her name?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Linda.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I remember, though.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She came from Prairie Grove and I taught her My Beautiful Home. If you didn't see her, if she was in the other room singing, you would think she was a Cherokee. She really learned to sing it well. She would lead that one. It was funny, one time, as for me, the others were older, of us singers. And I was the one in charge. I would say when we’re gonna practice. I called her one time, and told her we’re gonna be there Thursday night. She said, “Hawa, and got really happy. She said she was learning a new song, “that's what I'm going to want us to sing. You are going to have to learn this,” she told us. With that in mind, we went. “Now teach us that song you have been wanting us to learn.” She said, alright. It was Amazing Grace.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Amazing Grace?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: “Alright, start it then,” and she just looked at us. You know that? And I said, “We've sung it all our lives.”

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: That really was that song, Amazing Grace.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: It really is. If that don't touch you every time... You know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You dead, ain't it?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: That's true, that's true.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That which is medicine from the woods you have been told, this is the kind of medicine, this is that kind that helps you. Do you know what was making you better?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Even nowadays, if you knew what it was, would you all still be using that?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I can't find it anywhere anymore, things like that. Nobody hardly knows anything.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Mama was looking for something at Parson Hill, it was getting dark.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: It was dark.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: It was a little dark, you know. She told him, “Let's go get it, babe,” she said. She used to call Roy babe. “Babe, let's go get this medicine.” He would say, “It's dark now.” She would say, “I can still see.” She went and got it, and fixed and boiled it. She said she took a drink. Everywhere on her head was poison ivy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She was saying she could see good.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Mom about killed us, they said. They were - how would you say it? Scratching...

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They were scratching.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: They were scratching. I really don't forget that, it was funny.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Mom could speak Cherokee good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She could speak good, she was telling him.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Mom didn't speak English good. Cherokee, she could really throw it around.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: She was a funny old lady. It wasn't until they got better then I started laughing.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: It was everywhere.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: We were itching everywhere. If it was me, it would've killed me.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: As for me, I'm not allergic to it.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: If I even get near it, if I even stand close to it...

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Wasper, too, it would kill him.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, a wasper, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That oldest boy was like that, too. When he was going to school at Greasy, he got stung one time. It swelled up here [gesture], and his tongue swelled up. We took him to the doctor. He told us, “You brought him just in time.” He told us, “If y'all would have brought him just a little later, y'all would have lost your boy.”

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: That was bad.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: You have a boy that works at Memorial Hospital, ain't it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No, that is my nephew, is it Mike? Y'all probably know my son Keith.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: No, I don't know him.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You don't?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: What is his name? Did you say Keith?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, you know Keith.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I thought he said Heath. Keith, yes, I know Keith. Was it the one that my son bought the horse from, the white one?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is that your son?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I still have him.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: We still have Max.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You still own him? Do you know the reason I sold him? He did something strange one time I didn't know he’d got out. There was something coming on the ridge making a noise. When it came out, it was Max. He was running as fast as he could through the woods. We were standing by the house. He ran by fast as he could and went around the house. He got quiet. I thought, “What did he do? Why did he go off the hill that way?” I went around, and he was standing there just like a person would. He was peeking, doing this [gesture]. What he was doing was strange.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Did it scare you?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That was when I decided to sell him.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And you bought it.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: He is a good one.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: He tried to get mean for a while. Boy, that boy fell - he punched him really hard. He never did anything else.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: He is good now.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: He will just stand there, and you can crawl around his feet.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Without a saddle.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: You can pull his tail and comb him good, and he will stand there still.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He is old now, ain't it?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: With a washcloth, you can clean between his eyes.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He is friendly.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: He is good now, he is friendly.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I don't know if you know Tim? Tim was his name, we also raised him.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Tim, yeah. What ever happened to him?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He lives in Dodge, Kansas, and he still messes with horses. We have a picture of him and Max is standing there, and Tim, he is not on him. He is standing on the saddle. He was doing a whip like this [gesture], and Max was just like he was.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: It was him, Tim.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: It was him that came over.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: He just ran over there.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: One time he said, “There ole Max!” He started running when they put them on the back.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: He put his hands on his back.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: You know when they get off? That is what Max did when he got on.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He got on him.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Max took off running, and he just held on to his mane. They ran around everywhere for a little while, and they came back, and he got off.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: He is a friendly boy, that Tim.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: He has come over.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So y'all know him.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yes, he used to come to the house.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I have not seen him in a long time. Max really enjoys it when my boy and them come to the house. He would ride Max very quickly.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He really likes it. Still, he messes with horses.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: There have been a lot of people who have wanted to buy Max.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Still yet, ain't it?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I tell them it would be best if I just keep him.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He is pretty.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Even if he is by himself for a long time, he will come quickly. He is friendly.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Just whistle, ain't it?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: How would you say ‘whistle’?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: If I say it, it would be witsiyasvtlvelv.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: That is what I try to do is whistle at him. That is it, he still knows that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So he is still doing good.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: He is pretty. He is big.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: You might see him over at Dean Kimbles.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yes, I got him in a field at Dean Kimbles. He told me to put him in there.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: It is just on the side of the road you can see him.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He will be there.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: He probably has 60 or 65 acres to roam around in. He has a good place to walk around. I was telling you I should go get him, ain't it? And bring him to the house, but we have our grandchild who lives with us.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yes, we take care of babies.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: It is good, sometimes I don't know what I am doing.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: One, three, and five years old.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I will say, “What was I doing?” I will be asking them. Children are strange.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What do you do now? I don't work anywhere.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: He is disabled.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: It broke here [gesture]. I used to catch chickens for about 25 years.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, for that long.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: And so, it just suddenly came off. You - what they call - tear a rotor cuff. For me, it broke. It really tore up. I have had surgery three times. You know, they do a reverse shoulder implant when they put that ball in there. That was what they tried to fix the first time.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: But it didn't work, ain't it?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: It was just doing this [gesture]. I told them there was something going on, but they didn't believe me. I was going to that therapy. They were telling me, “If you pull it real hard, it will straighten out.” I was getting mad so I pulled it, and it broke apart.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: And surgery again.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: And then toward the doctor again, surgery again, and I was going to the doctor in Galela Kansas. I was going to a doctor all the way in Kansas.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: It was four hours away.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Workman’s comp... was wanting me to give up. They sent me way up there so I would. They tried to make it rough on me. They tried to starve me out. For a long time, they were not giving me any money. They were not helping me with anything, but then when they had to do it, we went that way.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I had surgery for the same thing, too. It was just one. I can't really use it for anything. For instance...

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I can't even throw a rock.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I can't either. If I'm going to throw it hard, I have to throw kind of like this [gesture]. I can't go like this [gesture].

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I am the same way. It really set me back when I was not able to work.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I felt really bad about it. I still haven't got used to it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you liked to work?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Yes, I like being outside.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Back then, did y'all eat things from the woods?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Deer meat, ain't it?

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: They really like deer meat, ain't it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So they do. What about mushrooms?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yesterday they cooked me morels. My niece girl came all the way from Arkansas. First, she called from a phone and said, “I have mushrooms I want to give you.” I said, “Well, bring them.” So Friday, she came all the way from Arkansas and brought them. It was just very little in a bag. Yesterday she cooked them. I ate them by myself. They just got two out. I ate them up by myself. Did your mother preserve things like that?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Oh yeah, poke salad, everything.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you learn to do that?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yes. She put them in jars, Momma did. You know those pickle jars? You stuff them with wild onion, poke salad.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you do that now?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: No, I don't.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You don't?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I am going to start, though. I was working for Cherokee Nation for 20 years, but then I got sick and I haven't worked since.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: That was bad, too. We were just thinking, she was in the hospital in Tulsa. She was talking about how we were going to pay the car. Thinking the FMLA should help, but they did not help with anything.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: They said, “You don't have enough hours.” I said I have been working with y'all 20 years.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: They denied her. They didn't help us with anything. “Working with Cherokee Nation,” they said, “if you ever get better, you can come back. That was all they said, thank you.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: They said I could come back.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: I felt really bad. I thought they were going to help us.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I liked what I did, taking care of elders, cooking for them.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: The elders really loved Norma. She watched them good.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: That was all they said. “We want Norma, we want Norma, gah-lee!” I won't go home till midnight. They really have come through some hard times and when you watch them good, it makes them better. It is bad for them when they are alone.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: It is sad for the elders when they don't have anyone to take care of them.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I watched Betty Glass. Watie and Betty, oh boy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Wasn't Watie here?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was here last week.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: That one is.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Betty is supposed to come next week.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Boy, they got sick, but they are better now. They got sick real bad.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Does Betty have dementia?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: A little bit.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: A little bit now, and Watie had heart surgery. I don't know, Betty was falling around.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Watie, too, ain't it? He was falling around.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That is what he was saying. He did not seem like he felt good.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I really want to go over there to make biscuits and gravy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I was surprised when Watie said when he got to Mankiller, they would not let him in unless he had security following him.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Gaw, how come?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I don't know.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Is he that bad?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He said he got a letter saying that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He said he got a letter that said that. So he said he can't go in without a security guard, they told him.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Were they just afraid he might fall or what?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: No, I guess he was getting on to them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He was getting on to the nurses.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don’t know if it's true, I don’t really know, he was thinking that the security guard was here. But it was just a worker who was helping him, Stan helped him. He thought they followed him all the way over here.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Watie came here.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yes, he came here.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He talked good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He talked good, we had a good talk.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: I really loved them; I really do, I really do. I miss them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He said he could not get her to get up, ain't it?

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Yeah, she don’t get around much. But when she does, she will be pretty when she gets out of bed.

segments.speaker: kenneth-littledeer
segments.translation: Mary Feathers was telling me about this here, and gave me the phone number and said you and your wife should go over there. Y'all will like it. You can talk in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Some are afraid.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They are afraid.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: Why? You know?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I guess.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: They don’t hardly talk. Yeah.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
segments.translation: It's kind of died down, really.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That is true.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Sometimes they will come in and say, “It's not going to be on TV, is it?”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Or they will be peeking in.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Sometimes I intentionally lie to them, and tell them that thing right there is the TV.

segments.speaker: norma-littledeer
